metadata.title: Does greater community involvement mean more parent-teacher interaction? Evidence from seven developing countries

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA-D 2015 microdata for seven low- and lower-middle-income countries and constructs school-level aggregates (e.g., the proportion of teachers receiving parent meeting demand) by calculating school means weighted using the school weights provided in the PISA-D dataset. In the regression models, the author states that final student survey weights are used to estimate all models, and the models are run separately for each country to examine cross-country differences. The paper does not report replicate-weight methodology (e.g., BRR/jackknife), and it instead reports robust standard errors in the regression tables/figures. Because the dependent variable is a bounded proportion derived from teacher reports, the weighting and aggregation steps are central to aligning the teacher-level information to the student-level analytic dataset.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic sample is drawn from PISA-D 2015 for 15-year-olds (mostly lower-secondary grades 7–10, plus about 11% from upper-secondary) in seven countries (Ecuador, Guatemala, Honduras, Paraguay, Cambodia, Senegal, Zambia). The outcome is teacher-reported parent meeting demand about students’ progress, converted to a school-level proportion (percentage of teachers receiving meeting demand) and merged with student-level predictors; teacher-level variables are aggregated to the school level using school weights so that schools are equally considered when selecting teachers. The paper imputes missing values for independent variables (background characteristics with generally <6% missingness) and includes dummies indicating whether each variable was imputed. The models are estimated separately for each country and include controls at student, school, and teacher levels (with teacher-level variables aggregated to the school level).

main_findings.performance_metrics: Country-specific OLS coefficients with robust standard errors; no ML metrics reported. Key reported results: community involvement coefficients are non-significant in all countries in the no-control and most full models; private school is significant in 6 of 7 countries (e.g., Ecuador: 0.21***; Honduras: 0.19**; Paraguay: 0.15**; Cambodia: 0.27**; Senegal: 0.27***; Zambia: 0.27***), while instructional resources become non-significant in most countries after adding school ownership (resources significant only for Paraguay in the full model). SES moderation: ownership×SES not significant in any country; resources×SES significant in Guatemala, Honduras, and Senegal (interaction coefficients: Guatemala 0.021*, Honduras 0.031**, Senegal 0.055**).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA-D 2015 data for 15-year-olds (teacher-reported parent meeting demand aggregated to the school level) across Ecuador, Guatemala, Honduras, Paraguay, Cambodia, Senegal, and Zambia, the study leveraged school type (private/public), instructional resources, and socioeconomic status (ESCS) to predict parent-teacher meeting demand, finding that school ownership/private status is significantly associated with higher parent meeting demand in six of seven countries while community involvement level is largely non-significant. This indicates that SBM-style community involvement alone may not reliably increase parent-teacher interaction, and that resource-linked school governance (e.g., private/fee-paying contexts) may be more consequential for enabling parents to request meetings, though the observational design limits causal interpretation.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses PISA-D 2015 data from seven developing countries (Ecuador, Guatemala, Honduras, Paraguay, Cambodia, Senegal, Zambia) to examine whether school-based management (SBM) community involvement is associated with parent-teacher interaction. The dependent variable is teacher-reported parent demand for personal meetings about students’ progress, converted into a school-level proportion and merged with student-level predictors; the models are estimated separately by country using OLS with robust standard errors, with logit-link GLM used as a robustness check. Across countries, community involvement level is not significant in most specifications, while school ownership/private status shows a significant positive association with meeting demand in six of seven countries. Instructional resources show significance in some models but largely lose significance once ownership is included, suggesting mediation by school ownership. The paper imputes missing independent variables and includes imputation dummies, but it does not fully document plausible-values combining rules for achievement covariates, and the observational correlational design prevents causal claims.
